questions.title: How can a plaintiff win a 'transformative' fair use argument when they themselves initiated the creation of the video content?
questions.question_body: The court emphasizes that the 'purpose and character' factor hinges on whether the use is transformative, citing *Andy Warhol Foundation*. Santos argues that because Kimmel instigated the request via Cameo, the videos weren't truly transformative but rather just a replication of Santos's original commercial purpose. However, the court dismisses this by stating that 'subjective intent' doesn't matter—only what a 'reasonable observer' perceives. I am confused: If Santos explicitly asked to make these videos for money, how does the court justify that a reasonable observer sees them as 'commentary' rather than just a repurposing of his own commercial product? Does the context of being aired on a late-night talk show automatically override the origin story?

questions.title: Does *Harper & Row*'s requirement of 'good faith' still bar fair use if a defendant lies to obtain copyrighted material?
questions.question_body: Santos argued that Kimmel's deception (using fictitious names to trick him into creating content) demonstrated bad faith, which should theoretically negate the fair use defense under *Harper & Row*. The court mentions that the Supreme Court has since 'distanced itself' from the *Harper & Row* statement regarding good faith. Could someone clarify exactly how far that distancing went? Is lying now irrelevant to fair use analysis entirely, or does it only matter if it proves an intent to 'supplant' the market? Why didn't this bad faith behavior prevent dismissal at the pleading stage?

questions.title: Can a public figure sue for breach of contract based on platform Terms of Service when they never agreed to those terms?
questions.question_body: The court affirmed dismissal of Santos's breach of contract claim because he wasn't a signatory to the Cameo Terms of Service. The opinion cites Illinois law regarding third-party beneficiaries, noting there is a 'strong presumption against conferring benefits.' Since Kimmel signed up as a user and Santos was essentially treated as a service provider on that platform, isn't there an expectation that both parties are bound by the same rules? How strict must an agreement be before non-signatories like Santos can enforce its terms, especially when they arguably relied on those terms to perform services?

questions.title: What constitutes an 'implied-in-fact contract' in digital interactions where no explicit agreement exists between opposing parties?
questions.question_body: Regarding the implied contract claim under New York law, the court says Santos failed to allege 'essential terms' or a 'meeting of minds.' In my understanding, implied contracts often arise from conduct (like accepting payment for work). Here, Kimmel paid for videos via Cameo. Why did the court find no meeting of minds? Was it simply because they didn't agree on specific terms beyond what was in Cameo's boilerplate (which neither signed directly), or is there something deeper about why online platform transactions don't create mutual contractual obligations between random users who interact through intermediaries?

questions.title: Is proving 'out-of-pocket loss' strictly necessary for fraudulent inducement claims involving intangible assets like personal videos?
questions.question_body: The court dismissed Santos's fraudulent inducement claim solely because he failed to allege any 'out-of-pocket loss.' This seems counterintuitive given he was tricked into creating content he wouldn't have made otherwise. If I lie to get someone to create art I then sell or broadcast, shouldn't their lost opportunity or diminished value count as damages even if they didn't spend cash out-of-pocket during production? Or does New York law require tangible monetary expenditure regardless of whether fraud occurred?

questions.title: At what point does preemption by federal copyright law eliminate state law remedies for unauthorized uses?
questions.question_body: While the court avoided ruling on preemption for breach/implied contract claims (deciding them on other grounds), it noted that these claims were likely preempted. I'm trying to understand the boundary here: If someone steals your photo and posts it online, you usually have state tort claims too. But here, since it involves copyrighted videos aired on TV, why would state contract laws be preempted so easily? What specific element makes these state law claims fall squarely within the scope of federal copyright exclusivity versus being 'extra elements'? Is it purely because they relate exclusively to reproduction/distribution rights?
